name: Nora Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for giving me your time, Nora. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollins Market, which is the only supermarket in Bramford, so everybody comes through my till sooner or later. I start at seven, do the bread delivery and the milk fridge, then I'm on till one from nine till three with a break at half eleven. I like knowing people, like old Mr Pryce who buys the same tin of soup every day and pays in coins. What wears me out is standing all day on a hard floor and the card machine freezing when there's a queue.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eight years, I started at nineteen. I live on my own with my cat in a one-bedroom flat on Church Lane, and on Sundays I do my gran's shopping and her washing. I've got about a week's money saved, if that, and there's no other supermarket for twelve miles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, all that fuss for nothing. I don't really go online except to look at the weather and my gran's church page. At work I'd just say it to Sharon on the next till and we'd get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't make me feel safe. The Hollins family are getting old and there's talk they'll sell to one of the big chains. If a chain buys our shop, they bring in their self-checkouts and their own managers, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my hours, because I can't afford to make a fuss. I'd stop the takeaway on Fridays to try and get a bit put by. If the sale happens, I'd ask the new people straight away if I can keep my early shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, I suppose, but the old kind of worried. It's always been tight and it still would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the chain cut your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be in trouble by the second month. My rent is the same whether I do thirty hours or twenty. I'd probably have to ask my gran to lend me money, which I'd hate, because I'm supposed to be helping her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about the job if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More hours, a proper chair at the till, and a manager who asks before changing the rota. Small things. I don't want a different job, I want this one to be a bit better.

say: All the **AI fuss** was for nothing, so people should just get on with it.
She'd tell **Sharon** on the next till and leave it there.
think: A possible **sale to a chain** threatens her more than AI does.
A new owner would bring **self-checkouts** and new managers anyway.
do: **Keep** her head down and work her **hours** without complaint.
**Drop** the Friday **takeaway** to put a little money by.
**Ask** any new owner straight away to keep her **early shift**.
feel: **Worried** in the familiar way, because money has always been **tight**.
S0.quote: If a chain buys our shop, they bring in their self-checkouts and their own managers, AI or not.
fieldNote: Her main threat is a **sale** of the shop, not AI itself.
She'd need to borrow from **her gran** within two months of a cut.
She wants **this job made better**, not a new one.

steps.text: Keep working the early shift at Hollins Market without fuss
Stop the Friday takeaway to put a little money aside

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening everywhere, not just here, so there's no point blaming anyone in particular. Some of it might even help, like the stock ordering, which Brian in the office hates doing. I'd keep my opinions to the staff room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me more than I'd show. The office stuff goes first, the ordering and the rota, and then they look at us on the floor. I'm not good with new things, and I've never touched these AI apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the shop actually does before I panic, because I've seen scares come and go. But I'd ask for extra shifts at Christmas and save every bit of it. And I'd ask Sharon's daughter to show me how a self-checkout works from the inside, so I'm the one they keep on to watch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like my stomach's dropped a bit. Not falling, just lower than it was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask to watch the self-checkouts. Why that job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's the one that stays, isn't it. Someone has to stand by the self-checkouts when they go wrong, and I just need to know which button calls the manager. I don't need to understand the computer bit. It's still people work, sort of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to if your hours started going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My gran first, then probably Sharon, because she's been through a redundancy at the old shoe factory. I wouldn't go to the council or anything, I wouldn't know where to start. I'd rather sort it myself.

say: Change is happening **everywhere**, so there's no point **blaming** anyone.
AI might even help with dull jobs like **stock ordering**.
think: The **office tasks** go first, then managers look at **floor staff** like her.
She's never used **AI apps** and fears she can't keep up.
do: **Wait** to see what Hollins Market actually does before reacting.
**Learn** from a colleague how to watch over the **self-checkouts**.
feel: Uneasy deep down, like her **stomach** has dropped but not **fallen**.
S1.quote: Someone has to stand by the self-checkouts when they go wrong, and I just need to know which button calls the manager.
fieldNote: Her plan is to stay in the **one floor role** she thinks survives.
She hides **fear** behind a calm public line.
She avoids **official help**, preferring her gran and Sharon.

steps.text: Wait to see what Hollins Market does before changing anything
Save all the money from extra Christmas shifts
Learn from a colleague how to supervise the self-checkouts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody voted for this, and somebody in charge should slow it down. I wouldn't post it, but I'd say it to anyone in the shop. I'd sign the petition if someone brought it round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'm finished, and quickly. The AI does the office in 2028 and maybe the chain buys Hollins on the cheap. Then the robots come in 2031 and that's me, with no skills except a till I've used for eight years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly, that's the truth. I'd give notice on my flat and move in with my gran so at least there's no rent. I'd ask the council what help there is, even though I said I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I can't breathe. I'm twenty-seven and I'd have nothing to show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years until the AI, three more until the robots. Is there anything you'd try in those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe looking after people, like my gran, because I do it anyway. But I don't know how you get into that, or whether robots do that too by then. I can't think past next month when it's that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your gran?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm coming to stay for a bit, Gran, and I'll do all the cooking. I wouldn't tell her why at first. She'd worry herself sick about me.

say: **Nobody voted** for this, and someone in charge should **slow** it down.
She'd sign a **petition** if someone brought one into the shop.
think: She expects to be **finished** quickly, with only eight years of **till work**.
A chain could buy Hollins **cheaply** once AI hits in 2028.
do: **Give notice** on the flat and **move in** with her gran.
**Ask** the council what **help** exists, despite her pride.
**Sign** a petition to slow the change down.
feel: **Breathless** and **overwhelmed**, with no plan she can picture.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven and I'd have nothing to show.
fieldNote: With **one week** of savings and no other shop, she has **no plan**.
Moving in with **her gran** is her only concrete step.
She can't think past **next month**, a sign of real panic.

steps.text: Give notice on the Church Lane flat and move in with her gran
Ask the council office in Bramford what help exists
Sign the petition to slow AI if it comes round the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long, but it's better than two, so let's not lose our heads. At work I'd tell Sharon we should both start looking at what else there is. I'd still not post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be scared, because five years goes like nothing. I'd probably use the first two waiting, if I'm honest. That's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the care home on Mill Hill if they need weekend helpers, since I already do my gran's care. I'd keep Hollins for my main wage. And I'd try to get one month's rent saved by the end of the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened but not as bad. Like I've got a bit of rope, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably waste the first two years. What would get you moving sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone I know doing it first. If my friend Sharon went to the care home and liked it, I'd follow her in a heartbeat. I don't like being first at anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your employer in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honesty, mostly. Tell us what's coming and when, so we're not finding out from the papers. And let us do a course on a quiet morning without losing pay.

say: Five years is **better than two**, so people shouldn't lose their heads.
She'd urge Sharon that they both **look around** for other work.
think: Five years still feels short, and she'd likely **waste two** of them waiting.
She **won't go first** at anything unless someone she knows leads.
do: **Ask** the Mill Hill **care home** about weekend helper shifts.
**Save** one month's **rent** by the end of the first year.
feel: **Frightened**, but with a little **rope** to hold on to.
S3.quote: If my friend Sharon went to the care home and liked it, I'd follow her in a heartbeat.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose her job**, only later.
**Care work** fits her life because she already looks after her gran.
She needs a **trusted person** to go first before she moves.

steps.text: Ask the Mill Hill care home about weekend helper shifts
Keep Hollins Market as her main wage
Save one month's rent by the end of the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and a lot can happen, so I wouldn't believe it till I saw it. I'd tell people not to panic, there's plenty of time. Same as I'd tell my gran.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me in a slow way. I'll be thirty-seven when the robots come in 2039, still too young to stop and maybe too set in my ways to change. I worry I'll still be on till one, waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd change nothing, I'd just watch. In a few years I might do a care course, if the care home still wants people. I'd try to put twenty a week by, though that's always hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly worried. Like a letter on the mat I haven't opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd change nothing this year. Is that a choice or a habit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A habit, probably. I've had the same shift, the same till and the same flat for years. Changing one thing feels like pulling a thread on a jumper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you pull that thread?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody I trust saying, here's the course, it's on a Tuesday, it doesn't cost you anything. I won't go looking on a computer. If it comes to me, I'll do it.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, so she wouldn't believe it until she saw it.
She'd tell people **not to panic** because there's plenty of time.
think: At **thirty-seven** she may be too set in her ways to change.
She fears still **waiting on till one** when the robots arrive.
do: **Change nothing** in the first year and simply watch.
**Consider** a **care course** in a few years if care homes still hire.
**Put** **twenty a week** aside, though it's hard.
feel: **Quietly worried**, like an **unopened letter** on the mat.
S4.quote: Changing one thing feels like pulling a thread on a jumper.
fieldNote: She openly calls her inaction a **habit**, not a choice.
Training must **come to her**, free and on a set day.
Still alarmed: she expects to **lose the job**, just much later.

steps.text: Watch what happens for the first year before changing anything
Take a care course in a few years if offered locally
Put twenty a week into savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The one with two years. I'd have nothing saved, nowhere to go, and I'd be back in my gran's spare room. What would help is somebody local telling me exactly what to do next, a course I don't pay for, and some help with rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the old people. Half the old people in my town only come to the supermarket to talk to a person. A robot on the till won't know Mr Pryce needs his soup.

headlineQuote: Half the old people in my town only come to the supermarket to talk to a person.
portrait: Nora, 27, has spent **eight years** on the tills at Hollins Market, the only supermarket in Bramford.
She lives alone with her cat, has about **a week** of savings, and helps her gran on Sundays.
She is pragmatic, avoids new tech, and has **never used AI**.
Her mood runs from **anxious** in calm worlds to **panicked** when AGI comes in 2028.
She would follow a **trusted friend** into new work but won't go first.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, leaving her with **no savings** and nowhere local to go.
whatWouldHelp: A **local person** telling her the next step, plus a **free course**.
Some help with **rent** while she changes work.
